lines.text: Can chlorine turn colourless iodide solution brown while iodine cannot do the reverse? Displacement reveals which halogen accepts electrons more readily.

Halogen molecules act as oxidising agents by accepting electrons, X two plus two electrons yields two X minus. Oxidising power decreases down Group seventeen, F two is greater than C L two is greater than B R two is greater than I two. A stronger halogen oxidises halide ions of any weaker halogen beneath it. For example, C L two aqueous plus two bromide aqueous yields two chloride aqueous plus B R two aqueous, chlorine is reduced and bromide is oxidised. Bromine displaces iodide but cannot displace chloride. Iodine displaces neither chloride nor bromide. Iodine present in a mixture dissolves in hexane and makes its layer purple, whether iodine was added directly or produced by displacement.
The oxidising trend predicts both displacement and the general decrease in vigour of halogen reactions with hydrogen.
Oxidising power, F two is greater than C L two is greater than B R two is greater than I two. A stronger halogen displaces a weaker halide. A purple hexane layer shows iodine is present.
Why does bromine displace iodide but fail to displace chloride?
Hydrogen can form a hydrogen halide with every halogen, yet the conditions and reaction vigour differ greatly.

Halogens combine with hydrogen to form hydrogen halides, H two gas plus X two gas yields two H X gas. Fluorine reacts explosively even in darkness. Chlorine reacts slowly in the dark but rapidly or explosively in light. Bromine reacts on heating, less vigorously than chlorine. Iodine reacts slowly and reversibly on heating. Overall reactivity with hydrogen decreases down Group seventeen. This is consistent with the decreasing oxidising power of the halogens, their tendency to accept electrons falls down the group. State the relevant light or heat condition when comparing specific reactions.
The hydrogen halides formed here have H X covalent bonds. Their varying strengths determine their thermal stabilities.
H two plus X two yields two H X. Reaction vigour generally falls from fluorine to iodine. Chlorine responds strongly to light, bromine and iodine need heating.
Why is iodine's reaction with hydrogen less vigorous than chlorine's?
Why does heating hydrogen iodide produce iodine more readily than heating hydrogen bromide? Compare the bonds that must break.

Thermal stability means resistance to decomposition on heating. Hydrogen halide thermal stability decreases H F is greater than H C L is greater than H B R is greater than H I. Down Group seventeen the halogen atom grows larger, the H X covalent bond length increases and its strength decreases. Less energy is needed to break the weaker bond, so decomposition becomes easier. The H F bond is strongest and H F is most thermally stable. The H I bond is weakest and H I is least thermally stable. Compare intramolecular H X bond strengths, rather than intermolecular forces, when explaining this trend.
The iodine produced on heating H I reflects the low thermal stability of H I, it does not reverse the oxidising power order of halogens.
Thermal stability is resistance to decomposition on heating. Stability, H F is greater than H C L is greater than H B R is greater than H I. H X bonds become longer and weaker down the group.

eleven point two The chemical properties of the halogen elements and the hydrogen halides.
In one breath.

Halogens become weaker oxidising agents down Group seventeen, and their reactions with hydrogen generally become less vigorous. Hydrogen halides become less thermally stable down the group because their H X bonds weaken.
Key ideas.

A halogen molecule, X two, acts as an oxidising agent when it accepts electrons to form halide ions, X two plus two electrons yields two X minus. Oxidising power decreases in the order F two is greater than C L two is greater than B R two is greater than I two. A halogen higher in this order oxidises the halide ions of a halogen below it. Thus chlorine displaces bromide and iodide, bromine displaces iodide, and iodine displaces neither chloride nor bromide. For example, C L two aqueous plus two bromide aqueous yields two chloride aqueous plus B R two aqueous. The halogen is reduced while the halide ion is oxidised. Do not confuse the reactivity of a halogen molecule with the reducing power of its halide ion, halide reducing power rises from fluoride to iodide.

Each halogen combines with hydrogen to form a hydrogen halide, H two gas plus X two gas yields two H X gas. Fluorine reacts explosively, even in the dark. Chlorine reacts slowly in darkness but rapidly or explosively in light. Bromine reacts with hydrogen on heating, less vigorously than chlorine. Iodine reacts slowly and reversibly on heating. The overall tendency toward less vigorous reaction down the group is consistent with decreasing halogen oxidising power, accepting electrons becomes less favourable. Reaction conditions matter, so quote the light or heat where relevant.

Thermal stability is resistance to decomposition on heating. It decreases H F is greater than H C L is greater than H B R is greater than H I. Down Group seventeen, the halogen atom gets larger, so the H X covalent bond becomes longer and weaker. Less energy is needed to break the bond, and the hydrogen halide decomposes more readily. For instance, hydrogen iodide can decompose to hydrogen and iodine on heating, whereas hydrogen bromide is more resistant under the same conditions. This trend concerns the covalent bond within each molecule, not the intermolecular forces between molecules.
Method.
For a displacement prediction, place both halogens in the oxidising power order. The higher halogen can oxidise the lower halide, write the new halide and the displaced halogen.
Balance the ionic equation by transferring two electrons, X two plus two yttrium minus yields two X minus plus Y two, provided X is above Y in the order.
For thermal stability, compare H X bond strengths. Name the stronger bond, then say which hydrogen halide requires more energy to decompose.
Worked example.

Predict the reaction when bromine is added to aqueous potassium iodide and explain it. Bromine is above iodine in oxidising power, so bromine oxidises iodide ions. B R two aqueous plus two iodide aqueous yields two bromide aqueous plus I two aqueous. Bromine is reduced and iodide is oxidised. Potassium ions are spectators.
Worked example, comparing thermal stability.

Compare H B R and H I on heating. The H bromine covalent bond is stronger than the H I bond, so more energy is needed to break H bromine. H B R therefore resists decomposition more and is more thermally stable than H I. Try the parallel comparison, Which is more thermally stable, H C L or H B R? Compare H chlorine and H bromine bond strengths first, then connect bond breaking to decomposition.
Traps.
Trap, Iodine displaces bromide because both are halogens. Why it's wrong, Iodine is below bromine in oxidising power. Instead, Compare their positions before writing products.

Trap, A purple hexane layer proves iodine was formed by displacement. Why it's wrong, Iodine initially added also dissolves in hexane. Instead, Count iodine already present as well as iodine produced.
Trap, H I is the most thermally stable because iodine is largest. Why it's wrong, The H I bond is the weakest H X bond. Instead, Link stronger bonds to greater thermal stability.
Exam technique.

For describe, give the order and the observable or reaction conditions. For explain, link the trend explicitly to oxidising power or H X bond strength. In displacement equations, include diatomic halogen molecules and balance both atoms and charge. If a question uses two solvent layers, identify which layer contains dissolved iodine before selecting its colour.
